Wrapped
RAPT
v.t. (pret. & pp.)
From Middle English wrappen, to fold or wind about, of uncertain Germanic origin. Webster 1828: to wind or fold together; to involve; to cover by winding something round. Scripture uses it at the two ends of our Lord’s earthly life — the swaddling bands and the grave clothes.

Biblical Definition

The word binds the manger to the tomb. Luke records the nativity in the plainest terms: she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger (Luke 2:7), and the angel makes those bands the appointed evidence: Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger (Luke 2:12). The sign of the Messiah is not a crown but a cloth. Thirty-three years later John looks into an empty sepulchre and notices how the linen lay: the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself (John 20:7). The detail is evidential. A robbed grave is a ransacked grave; this one is orderly, the head-cloth folded by itself, as of a man who rose and had no need of haste. Between manger and tomb the word appears in Jonah’s prayer from the deep: the weeds were wrapped about my head (Jonah 2:5) — and our Lord Himself made Jonah’s three days the one sign He would give. He who was wrapped in swaddling bands was wrapped in grave clothes, and left them folded.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WRAP as to wind or fold together; to involve; to cover by winding or folding something about a thing; hence WRAPPED, involved, enveloped, folded about.

WRAP, v.t. — To wind or fold together; as, to wrap close.

To involve; to cover by winding or folding something round.

To comprise; to contain; as, this is wrapped up in the general question.

WRAPPED, pp. — Wound; folded; enveloped; involved.

Middle English wrappen; compare lap, to fold, and envelop.

Key Scripture

Luke 2:7 — "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn."

Luke 2:12 — "And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger."

John 20:7 — "And the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself."

Jonah 2:5 — "The waters compassed me about, even to the soul: the depth closed me round about, the weeds were wrapped about my head."

Modern Corruption

Modern nativity sentiment turns the swaddling clothes into a picture of cosiness; Scripture makes them a sign of humiliation, and the folded napkin of John 20:7 a sober evidence of resurrection.

expand to see more

The swaddling bands are not decoration. They are the first article of the Son’s humiliation after the incarnation itself: the eternal Word, by whom the worlds were made, bound in cloth like any other infant and laid where beasts feed. Luke names the reason without softening it — because there was no room for them in the inn. When the carol tradition turns this into rustic charm, the doctrine goes out of it. The angel gave the bands as the identifying sign: the shepherds would know Messiah not by splendour but by poverty. That is the pattern of the whole ministry, and the 1689 Confession states it plainly in its chapter on the mediator — He took our nature with all its essential properties and common infirmities, yet without sin.

John 20:7 has been pressed by some into ingenious readings about ancient napkin-folding customs; the text needs no such help. The evidential point is simply order. Grave-robbers do not unwind a body and leave the head-cloth folded apart. John saw it, and the next verse says he believed. The Reformed doctrine of the resurrection rests on bodily, public, examinable fact — the same body that was wrapped, now risen — not on the disciples’ inner experience. Any account that relocates the resurrection into the believer’s subjectivity has abandoned what John reports himself to have looked at and handled.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sparganoo (G4683), to wrap in swaddling bands; entulisso (G1794), to wrap up, to roll together; Hebrew chabash (H2280), to bind or wrap about.

expand to see more

Greek sparganoo (G4683) — to swathe in strips of cloth; used only of the infant Christ, in Luke 2:7 and Luke 2:12.

Greek entulisso (G1794) — to roll or fold together; used of the head napkin in John 20:7.

Greek eneileo (G1750) — to wind in, used by Mark of the linen at the burial (Mark 15:46).

Hebrew chabash (H2280) — to bind, to wrap about; used of Jonah’s weeds and of binding up wounds.

Hebrew suph (H5488) — weeds or reeds, the sea-growth wrapped about Jonah’s head (Jonah 2:5).

Usage

"Wrapped him in swaddling clothes (Luke 2:7) — the first article of the Son’s humiliation after the incarnation itself."

"Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes (Luke 2:12) — the appointed sign of Messiah is a cloth, not a crown."

"Wrapped together in a place by itself (John 20:7) — a robbed grave is ransacked; this one is orderly."
